lesson.title: The Célébrer Trap
lesson.subtitle: Strip, don't trim — discrimination drills for the -ation engine

hook.title: Where the Mind Cuts Corners
hook.content: The engine's one failure mode: cutting only part of -ation. Célébrater. Organisater. The mind sees -ate in the English verb and keeps it. This gym exists to catch that corner-cutting in a safe room — strip the noun whole, every time.

pattern.title: Convert the Noun, Not the Verb
pattern.content: The reliable path: find the English -ation noun first, convert IT to French, then strip it. Celebrate? Ask: celebration? Yes → célébration → célébrer. The noun is the test — if there's no -ation noun, don't trust the jump. (Reserve → reservation → réserver. Invite → invitation → inviter.)
pattern.trap_note: Participer, not participater. Visiter, not visitater. The English -ate is Latin -āre's ghost — French kept the ghost only in the noun.

exercises.explanation: Strip -ation whole: célébration → célébrer. The -ate in English is a false friend of the engine.
participation → participer. The same strip-whole law.
reservation → réserver — the é rides along, marking the stress.

exercises.idea: you want to reserve a table — for tonight
exercises.meaning: I want to reserve a table

vocab_hints.note: la table is feminine — a table is une table

exercises.explanation: je veux réserver une table — and une is la's indefinite sibling: same gender, one glance.

summary.outcome: Convert through the noun, not the verb — and never trust an -ate jump.

use_example.english: I want to reserve — not to 'celebrater'.

summary.takeaway: The -ation noun is the test and the vehicle: convert it, then strip it whole.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([302] Je veux + Infinitive Gym): see how The Célébrer Trap leads directly into Je veux + Infinitive Gym.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I want to reserve a table" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je veux réserver une table" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Célébrer Trap.

célébrer.etymology_derivation: célébration → célébrer. The trap: not *célébrater — the whole -ation goes before -er arrives.

confirmer.etymology_derivation: confirmation → confirmer. Strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the verb.

organiser.etymology_derivation: organisation → organiser. One S in French, even where English writes Z.

réserver.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.

inviter.context_translation: Do you want to invite Marie?

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

table.etymology_derivation: Latin tabula 'board, plank'. English borrowed the French word whole — remember it is feminine: la table.

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.
